extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/epistemology (readers of Locke)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Locke's criteria for judging ideas (clear, distinct, confused) and for judging moral actions by their conformity to rules (divine, civil, opinion). Useful for analyzing concepts, moral evaluation, and clarity in philosophical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Relation
rubrics_metrics.description: The conformity or disagreement of voluntary actions to a rule to which they are referred, and by which they are judged of; called a moral relation because it denominates our moral actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human actions are mixed modes composed of ends, objects, manners, circumstances; beyond naming them we must judge whether such actions are morally good or bad by comparing their composition to a rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Good and Evil
rubrics_metrics.description: Good and evil are nothing but pleasure or pain, or that which occasions or procures pleasure or pain to us; MORAL GOOD AND EVIL is the conformity or disagreement of our voluntary actions to some law whereby good or evil is drawn on us from the will and power of the law-maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral good/evil is tied to reward and punishment appointed by a lawgiver, not merely natural consequences of actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law must carry enforcement (rewards/punishments)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule set to the free actions of men must have some enforcement of good and evil annexed to it; otherwise it is in vain to suppose such a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a law-maker lacks power to reward compliance and punish deviation by non-natural goods/evils, the rule cannot function as law. This is presented as the true nature of law properly so called.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three sorts of moral laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws to which men compare actions to judge rectitude are three: (1) the Divine law, (2) the Civil law, (3) the law of Opinion or Reputation (fashion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each law has different enforcements and yields different moral denominations (sin/duty, criminal/innocent, virtue/vice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine law as touchstone of sin and duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The Divine law, whether promulgated by nature or revelation, is the sole true touchstone of moral rectitude; by comparing actions to it men judge the most considerable moral good or evil (sin or duty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: God has right, goodness, wisdom, and power to enforce by rewards/punishments of infinite weight, so divine law determines ultimate moral status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil law as measure of crimes and innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Civil law, set by the commonwealth, is the rule to judge whether actions are criminal or innocent; it is enforced by the commonwealth's power to protect and to punish (life, liberty, goods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the practical rule people commonly apply when deciding legality and civic culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of opinion/reputation as measure of virtue and vice
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of opinion or reputation is the tacit consent of a society which attributes praise or blame, and so determines what each society calls virtue or vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue and vice here track public esteem and disesteem; what is praiseworthy in a society is called virtue regardless of other standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue and vice commonly measured by public esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is everywhere that which is thought praiseworthy in a society; nothing else but what has the allowance of public esteem is called virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although different societies may differ, public approbation generally corresponds with the unchangeable rule of right and wrong (divine law) because public esteem tends to encourage what benefits people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement of opinion is commendation and discredit
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of fashion (opinion) is enforced by commendation and disgrace, which are powerful motives causing most men to conform to the opinions/rules of those they converse with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social censure and loss of reputation are significant penalties; many prefer social approbation to concern for divine or civil penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality as relation of voluntary actions to rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Morality consists in the relation of voluntary actions to some rule (divine, civil, or opinion); moral goodness or evil is simply conformity or disagreement of actions to that rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions are judged by whether the simple ideas composing them correspond to the ideas required by the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions considered absolutely vs as relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral actions may be regarded either absolutely (as mixed modes composed of particular simple ideas) or as ideas of relation (as good/bad in relation to a rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An action like duelling is a positive mode in itself but can be sin, virtue, or a capital crime depending on which rule (divine, fashion, civil) is used for judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denominations of actions often mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the positive idea of an action and its moral relation are often expressed by the same name, people are led to conflate the action and its moral status (e.g., 'stealing' may name both the mixed mode and its moral gravity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conflation leads to mistaken judgments; one must separate the positive idea of an action from its relation to rules when assessing moral rectitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: All relations terminate in simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: All relation is ultimately founded on the simple ideas we have from sensation or reflection; relative words ultimately terminate in simple ideas (e.g., 'honey is sweeter than wax' terminates in sweetness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To analyze relations, trace compound or proportional relations back to the simple ideas composing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation is perceivable even if the rule is false
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of relation (agreement or disagreement) can be perceived by comparing an action with a rule, whether that rule is true or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measuring by a wrong rule may make one judge amiss of moral rectitude, but one is not mistaken about the relation the action bears to that (possibly wrong) rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear vs Obscure ideas (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple ideas are CLEAR when the objects from which they were taken present them in well-ordered sensation and memory; OBSCURE when they lack sufficient presentation or have faded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains via sight: light discovers objects — an idea is obscure when not presented with sufficient 'light' (vividness) in perception or memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct vs Confused ideas (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A DISTINCT idea is one in which the mind perceives a difference from all other ideas; a CONFUSED idea is not sufficiently distinguishable from another from which it ought to be different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctness concerns perceivable differences; confusion arises relative to names and the distinctions names are supposed to mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurity in simple ideas arises chiefly from either dull organs (impaired perception), very slight/transient impressions, or weakness of memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to poor impressions in wax; poor sensory input or retention makes ideas obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion default: too few simple ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex idea made up of too few simple ideas (especially ones common to other things) is liable to confusion, failing to be distinguished from related ideas (e.g., a scant idea of 'leopard' could be confused with 'lynx').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid confusion, include the specific differences (more simple ideas) that separate related concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion default: simple ideas jumbled disorderly
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a complex idea has enough parts, if those parts are so jumbled that one cannot discern order, the idea appears confused insofar as it cannot be clearly assigned to one name rather than another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a distorted picture may be confused when applied to a specific name (man, Caesar) until reordered or properly viewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion default: simple ideas mutable and undetermined
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea is confused when its content varies from one occasion to another (mutable/undetermined), so it cannot be steadily assigned to one name (e.g., unstable notions of 'church' or 'idolatry').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency in the precise combination of simple ideas applied to a name prevents this form of confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion always concerns two ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusion arises from the difficulty to separate two ideas that should be separated; one must examine which other idea it is being confounded with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolving confusion requires identifying the proximate idea it risks being confounded with and clarifying distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas may be distinct in one part and confused in another
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas, being collections of many simple ideas, can be very clear and distinct in some parts yet obscure or confused in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis of complex ideas should examine each constituent part for clarity and distinctness rather than treating the whole as uniformly clear or confused.
